target: AG1’s claim that AI improves economic well-being by complementing human work and that retraining can reduce displacement harms.
objection: AI often automates or substitutes for human labor and shifts gains toward system owners/deployers, which can reduce the economic well-being of workers and smaller businesses rather than preserve it.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can make education and professional work easier without broader downside.
objection: Ready-made AI answers and assistance can reduce opportunities for students and adults to practice independent reasoning, thereby weakening critical thinking skills.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can help marginalized groups and society without reinforcing bias.
objection: Because AI learns from historical data that contains discrimination, it can reproduce and amplify racist patterns, harming racial minorities.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can improve workplace safety and society overall.
objection: AI often depends on collecting and inferring personal data, which creates serious privacy risks such as exposure of sensitive information and increased surveillance.

target: AG2’s claim that AI deployments are inevitably too opaque to verify or challenge.
objection: AI can be deployed with explanations, audit trails, and appeal or review processes, including human oversight, so affected people can scrutinize and contest AI-influenced outcomes rather than facing unavoidable opacity.

target: AG2’s assumption that hard-to-challenge AI necessarily leads to persistent harms in high-stakes settings.
objection: If AI outputs are subject to appeals, audits, and human or institutional review, then errors and harmful outcomes have practical routes for detection and correction, so hard-to-challenge AI is not necessary for persistent harm.

target: AG2’s claim that AI will persistently worsen discrimination against racial minorities because biased outputs are hard to contest.
objection: Bias and discrimination can be identified through audits and corrected when contested decisions are reviewed and amended, so contestability and review can reduce persistent discriminatory impact.

target: AG2’s conclusion that opaque AI is not good for society overall.
objection: Because contestability and review can prevent harmful errors and discriminatory impacts from persisting, AI can avoid the broad ‘not good’ outcome and still be good for society overall.

target: AG1’s reply that explanation, audits, and appeals remove the privacy problem.
objection: Privacy harms arise from data collection and incorporation into AI systems, and decision-level review does not eliminate the core privacy risks created once personal data has been collected and used.

target: AG1’s claim that challenge mechanisms mean AI does not pose ongoing privacy danger.
objection: Even when users can challenge outputs, AI can still pose dangerous privacy risks because the underlying data exposure and surveillance potential remain ongoing.

target: AG1’s claim that bias mitigation plus appeals can prevent persistent discrimination.
objection: Discriminatory impacts can re-emerge across new contexts and after model updates, and audits or appeals cannot feasibly test every subgroup in every deployment, so mitigation may fail to prevent persistent discrimination.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be made good for society despite discrimination and privacy concerns.
objection: A technology is not good for society when it predictably causes ongoing harms to privacy and racial equity, and those harms can persist even under the proposed review regime.

target: AG1’s claim that appeal/audit systems prevent AI from causing economic harm.
objection: AI deployment can restructure workflows, labor demand, and bargaining power in ways that disadvantage workers and smaller businesses even when individual decisions are reviewable.

target: AG1’s claim that decision-level appeals and audits can avert economic harm.
objection: Structural harms from automation and changing labor or market conditions are not mainly caused by a single incorrect decision, so appeals and audits cannot adequately prevent or reverse them.

target: AG1’s conclusion that contestability makes AI socially good overall.
objection: Because workers’ economic well-being and business viability are central to social good, widespread economic harm that contestability cannot undo makes AI not good for society overall.

target: AG1’s claim that AI-supported learning tools can strengthen critical thinking.
objection: Many AI tools give ready-made answers or drafting help in a way that reduces the need to practice independent reasoning in learning and everyday decision-making, so AI can undermine critical thinking skills.

target: AG1’s claim that output review eliminates the critical-thinking concern.
objection: The harm is that AI reduces the user’s own reasoning practice, which happens during use rather than as a single incorrect output that can later be appealed, so contestability does not remove the critical-thinking harm.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s critical-thinking effects are not socially bad overall.
objection: If AI predictably undermines critical thinking in students and adults, then it is not good for society even if some outputs are reviewable afterward.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily reduces real evaluation and deference to AI outputs undermines critical thinking.
objection: AI can be used for interactive coaching that gives hints, requires users to propose answers, and asks follow-up questions, forcing users to reason rather than passively accept AI outputs.

target: AG2’s claim that AI use predictably weakens critical thinking.
objection: When users must attempt and justify their own reasoning to get help, they practice independent problem-solving and evaluation, which supports critical thinking rather than reliably undermining it.

target: AG2’s overall conclusion that AI is not good for society because of critical-thinking harms.
objection: If AI can be deployed in ways that strengthen critical thinking, then the claim that AI is socially bad on the basis of critical-thinking harm is not generally warranted.

target: AG1’s claim that interactive coaching is a realistic enough deployment mode to save AI’s critical-thinking case.
objection: The relevant question is AI’s typical large-scale impact, and interactive coaching is costly and constraining, so it is unlikely to be the dominant deployment pattern for most high-volume AI products aimed at convenience and efficiency.

target: AG1’s claim that possible coaching-style uses show AI is good overall.
objection: If AI is not generally deployed in a way that reliably increases genuine independent reasoning, then the critical-thinking objection remains relevant and the existence of coaching-style designs does not establish that AI is good for society overall.

target: AG1’s claim that coaching-style AI removes broader social concerns.
objection: Even coaching-like interfaces still rely on underlying data-driven automated decision-making that creates privacy exposure and biased outcomes, so changing the interaction style does not remove AI’s main social harms.

target: AG1’s overall positive verdict based on coaching-style AI.
objection: A technology is not good for society when its dominant uses fail to reliably improve reasoning for the public and significant underlying harms such as privacy and bias persist.

target: AG1’s claim that fairness measures and privacy safeguards can reduce AI harms enough to support an overall positive verdict.
objection: Meaningful mitigation requires sustained governance in real deployments, including ongoing bias testing, data minimization, consent and access controls, and enforcement that continues across model updates.

target: AG1’s claim that safeguards will be consistently implemented at scale.
objection: In practice, organizations often prioritize speed, scale, and performance, which makes them likely to apply only partial or inconsistent safeguards rather than full ongoing governance.

target: AG1’s claim that AI harms can be prevented in practice through governance.
objection: If safeguards are partial or inconsistent across deployments and model updates, discrimination and privacy risks are likely to persist rather than be eliminated, especially harming racial minorities and privacy-sensitive individuals.

target: AG1’s overall conclusion that AI is good for society when benefits remain and harms are supposedly mitigable.
objection: When key harms persist in realistic deployment conditions, a technology is not good for society overall even if some benefits remain.

target: AG1’s claim that standardized monitoring and audits make scalable AI governance feasible.
objection: Although governance can be standardized, it still requires durable ongoing oversight and compliance, not just one-time design changes, so mitigation remains costly and operationally demanding.

target: AG1’s claim that standardized compliance prevents persistent harms at scale.
objection: Because real deployments face incentives to cut corners, safeguards are unlikely to be consistently implemented across all deployments and updates, so discrimination and privacy risks may still persist.

target: AG1’s claim that AI’s broad benefits outweigh mitigable harms.
objection: If AI’s key harms persist in practice, then the overall verdict cannot be positive merely because benefits exist; persistent discrimination and privacy harms still make AI not good for society overall.

target: AG1’s claim that broad benefits across convenience, work, accessibility, and safety make AI good overall.
objection: AI’s benefits in convenience, work support, accessibility, and safety do not by themselves cancel the serious harms to privacy, racial equity, and economic well-being that AI can produce.

target: AG2’s claim that AI privacy harms cannot be meaningfully reduced because data collection already occurred.
objection: Privacy harm is not irreversible merely because sensitive signals were extracted; retention limits, access controls, consent and purpose controls, and post-issue remediation can limit and correct exposure over time.

target: AG2’s claim that discrimination will keep worsening despite monitoring.
objection: Bias testing and subgroup-aware monitoring can be designed to track performance across versions and trigger corrective actions, so discrimination can be reduced over time rather than persistently worsening.

target: AG2’s claim that workforce support cannot offset AI’s economic disruption.
objection: Economic disruption from automation can be mitigated by transition support and by productivity gains that create complementary human work, so AI need not persistently increase disruption overall.

target: AG2’s overall negative verdict under the integrated decision rule.
objection: If the broad-benefit cluster is present and the three persistent-harm pathways need not reliably persist when safeguards and transition support are implemented, then AI is good for society overall.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy controls can stay meaningful despite updates and changing deployments.
objection: Because AI deployments continually change through model updates, retraining, and new integrations, meaningful privacy control cannot be guaranteed to persist if it depends on stable conditions.

target: AG1’s claim that users can maintain privacy control over time through controls and safeguards.
objection: If users cannot reliably re-consent or re-opt out when systems change, later updates and integrations can reintroduce sensitive inferences and secondary uses without renewed user control.

target: AG1’s claim that subgroup-aware monitoring and corrective updates prevent persistent discrimination.
objection: Bias and discrimination risks can shift with updates and new data uses, and ongoing monitoring cannot guarantee that discrimination will not persist across all future contexts or that harms will be corrected fast enough for affected minorities.

target: AG1’s claim that persistent harms are not established as prevailing when safeguards and transition support exist.
objection: If AI can persistently worsen discrimination, undermine privacy control, and increase economic disruption, then it is not good for society overall under the integrated decision rule.

target: AG2’s claim that continual change defeats privacy governance.
objection: Meaningful privacy control does not require a stable system; enforceable user controls and fresh privacy impact checks can be applied at runtime and at each update or integration, with blocking or rollback if exposure expands beyond consent.

target: AG2’s claim that updates make discrimination persistence inevitable.
objection: Bias risks can be handled by pre-release fairness testing for each version, and versions that worsen subgroup outcomes can be blocked or rolled back so discrimination need not persist across model changes.

target: AG2’s overall negative verdict based on persistent harms.
objection: If broad benefits are present and the three persistent-harm pathways need not reliably persist when safeguards and transition support are implemented, then AI is good for society overall.

target: AG1’s claim that user-facing controls can preserve privacy even if users do not understand every inference.
objection: Meaningful privacy control requires that users understand what sensitive data and inferences are used and how to limit exposure in practice, but AI systems are often too opaque for ordinary users to do this effectively.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy impact checks and rollback can maintain privacy control over time.
objection: If users cannot understand or control current sensitive inferences, then impact checks and rollback cannot reliably prevent privacy harm from persisting in real use.

target: AG1’s claim that subgroup-aware monitoring and rollback prevent discrimination from persisting.
objection: Bias testing can miss new contexts or distribution shifts, and rollback only stops future releases; it does not undo discriminatory harms already imposed on racial minorities.

target: AG1’s claim that transition support plus productivity gains prevent persistent economic disruption.
objection: AI automation can structurally change labor demand and business viability, and workforce transition support is often too limited to eliminate the large-scale displacement and reduced agency caused by widespread AI adoption.

target: AG1’s overall positive verdict based on safeguardable harms.
objection: A technology is not good for society overall when it persistently worsens discrimination, undermines privacy control, and increases economic disruption, which AI can do in realistic deployment conditions.

target: AG2’s claim that continual change prevents privacy control from being maintained.
objection: Meaningful privacy control only requires enforceable current controls, and AI systems can be governed so that each update or integration is privacy-checked and blocked or rolled back if it expands exposure beyond what users consented to.

target: AG2’s claim that update-driven change makes discrimination persistence unavoidable.
objection: Bias risks after updates can be handled with version-specific subgroup testing and rollback, so versions that worsen subgroup outcomes need not be released and discrimination need not persistently worsen.

target: AG2’s overall negative verdict under the integrated rule.
objection: If privacy control and discrimination do not persistently worsen across updates, then the persistent-harm cluster need not prevail, and with broad benefits present AI is good for society overall.

target: AG2’s claim that ordinary users must fully understand every internal inference to have meaningful privacy control.
objection: Meaningful privacy control can be secured by enforceable governance—limits on collection and retention, restricted access to sensitive inferences, deletion, purpose limitation, and remedies—without users understanding every internal inference.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy safeguards cannot prevent persistent privacy harm.
objection: When enforceable constraints exist at the points of collection, retention, and downstream use, privacy impact checks and update gating can prevent sensitive exposure from persisting across deployments.

target: AG2’s claim that discrimination will still persist despite subgroup monitoring and rollback.
objection: Bias testing plus corrective retraining and retroactive redress can reduce discriminatory impacts even across distribution shifts, and re-emergence does not mean discrimination must prevail overall.

target: AG2’s claim that the integrated negative verdict follows from realistic persistent harms.
objection: If privacy control can be maintained and discriminatory harms can be corrected or remediated over time, the opponent has not established that the persistent-harm cluster prevails against the broad-benefit evidence, so AI is good for society overall.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s broad benefits do not suffice for an overall positive verdict.
objection: AI reliably generates broad social benefits in everyday life, education/work, disability accessibility, and workplace safety, which satisfy the broad-benefit cluster relevant to the overall judgment.

target: AG2’s assumption that the negative verdict requires only plausible harm pathways rather than prevailing harms.
objection: Under the integrated decision rule, a negative verdict requires strong evidence that discrimination, privacy control, and economic disruption are all persistent, prevailing harms across deployments, not just plausible risks.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms overwhelm its benefits.
objection: The target has not established that the persistent-harm cluster prevails against the broad-benefit evidence across deployments, so the overall negative conclusion is not supported.

target: AG2’s claim that economic disruption is inevitable and persistent.
objection: AI can increase productivity and shift labor toward complementary work, so economic disruption is not inevitable and depends on whether workers and businesses can transition to the new task landscape.

target: AG2’s claim that transition support cannot prevent lasting economic harm.
objection: Workforce transition support such as retraining, wage supports, and redeployment assistance can help workers and smaller firms move into complementary tasks, preventing persistent displacement and reduced agency.

target: AG2’s overall negative verdict based partly on economic disruption.
objection: If economic disruption need not persist overall and AI also provides broad benefits in convenience, work, accessibility, and safety, then the integrated negative conclusion does not hold and AI can be good for society overall.

target: AG2’s claim that users must understand every internal inference for privacy control.
objection: Privacy control is about enforceable limits on collection, retention, and use, not full user understanding of internals, so governance can make privacy protection meaningful even when users cannot foresee every inference.

target: AG2’s claim that privacy harms inevitably persist across deployments.
objection: When enforceable constraints and update gating limit sensitive exposure at collection and downstream use, privacy harm need not persist across deployments.

target: AG2’s claim that racial discrimination must persist as an overall harm.
objection: Discrimination can re-emerge, but corrective governance, subgroup monitoring, and retroactive redress mean persistent worsening is not established as a prevailing overall harm.

target: AG2’s overall conclusion that AI is not good for society because harms persist.
objection: If broad benefits are strong and the persistent-harm cluster is not established as prevailing, then AI is good for society overall under the integrated decision rule.
